newsitem.title: MEXICO: New poll has Mexico govt party headed for defeat.
newsitem.headline: New poll has Mexico govt party headed for defeat.

text.p: An opinion poll published on Wednesday showed President Ernesto Zedillo's party heading for defeat in congressional elections on July 6.

The poll, by the Guadalajara University's Opinion Studies Centre (CEO) showed Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) had just 30.7 percent support -- way below what it needs to keep its lower house majority under Mexico's complicated electoral system.
The poll said the conservative National Action Party (PAN) was almost level with the PRI on 30.0 percent, while the left-wing PRD had 20.9 percent.

Support for Zedillo himself was much higher than for his party. The president scored a 64.9 percent approval rating, up nearly five points from a similar poll conducted last December, though his economic policies were not so popular.
The PRI's huge Senate majority is not threatened because only a quarter of that chamber is up for election next month. The whole of the lower house is being renewed.
The ruling party's biggest problem with voters was corruption, CEO said. Of those who refused to vote PRI, nearly two-thirds said their main reason was that it was corrupt.
Some 4.8 percent expressed a preference for small parties in the congress survey, while 13.6 percent did not reply or did not know.

CEO's survey, taken June 20 on a sample of 3,677 Mexicans nationwide, had a two percent margin of error. It differed sharply from other national opinion polls which have put the PRI well clear of the opposition.
A survey by Reforma newspaper published June 19 gave the PRI 32 percent, the PAN 24 percent and the PRD 16 percent, with 23 percent undecided or not replying.
Asked about the CEO poll, a senior government official told Reuters he believed it was wrong.
"Our own polls, which we believe are accurate, show us just around or just short of the level we need for a majority," he said. "We are very near to obtaining a majority in Congress".

CEO stressed that because of the electoral system for the lower house, which mixes proportional representation and first-past-the-post districts, it could not exactly predict how its poll results would translate into seats in congress.
Significantly in a country with a history of electoral fraud, the poll also showed that recent government reforms appeared to have calmed fears of dirty tricks.
Nearly half those polled (49.3 percent) said they trusted in the impartiality of the newly independent Federal Electoral Institute running the vote, while only 35.5 percent said they did not.
